newsitem.title: UK: Book on McDonald's libel case due before verdict.
newsitem.headline: Book on McDonald's libel case due before verdict.

text.p: The story of the libel case that burger giant McDonald's slapped on two cash-strapped activists, resulting in a 313-day trial and spawning an Internet website, will soon be available as a book.

Judge Rodger Bell's verdict in Britain's longest trial isn't expected until May, but "McLibel: Burger Culture on Trial" --written by a British journalist with the collaboration of the two defendants -- will be in the bookshops in April, publishers MacMillan said on Thursday.
"It was our plan to have it published before the judgment," said spokeswoman Antonia Bailey.

Single father Dave Morris and Helen Steel, a part-time barmaid, have devoted nearly four years of their lives defending themselves against charges that they libelled the $30 billion-a-year corporation in a fact sheet.

The leaflet, accusing McDonald's of promoting an unhealthy diet, ruining the environment, being hostile to trade unions and exploiting children and workers, was produced in the mid-1980s by London Greenpeace, a little-known group with no relation to Greenpeace International.
Three members of the group apologised to McDonald's after receiving writs, but Morris and Steel decided they wanted their day, or as it turned out years, in court.
"It's not our story, it's a book about our story," Morris told Reuters, emphasising that neither he nor Steel had any editorial control. "It's very much a look about both sides of the trial."
Mike Love, McDonald's European spokesman, said the company did not contribute to the book and would not do so in advance of any judgement.

If the judge rules against them, Morris and Steel, who conducted their own defence in the David and Goliath case after being denied legal aid, say they will launch an appeal and may take the case to the European Court of Human Rights.
"We've already made strong submissions in our closing speech about European law. We will be definitely planning to go to the European Court (if an appeal fails)," said Morris.
The defendants will claim the libel laws in Britain are oppressive because they were denied legal aid and a jury trial, after the judge ruled the case was too complicated.

Since Morris and Steel are virtually penniless, McDonald's cannot hope to recoup the costs of the trial, estimated to have cost millions of pounds (dollars). The company said it wants a retraction and an injunction prohibiting the defendants from repeating the allegations.
